sections.title: Case Definition
sections.content: Vitiligo is a chronic, acquired autoimmune skin disorder characterized by well-demarcated hypopigmented or depigmented macules and patches resulting from the selective destruction of melanocytes in the epidermis. It may affect the skin, mucous membranes, and hair follicles, and can be associated with systemic autoimmune conditions such as thyroiditis, uveitis, and sensorineural hearing loss. Before addressing vitiligo, it is important to understand the basic target cell that is affected by the disease and for that a basic overview of the melanin pathway is essential. Melanin is formed from the essential amino acids tyrosine and phenylalanine through a series of enzymatic steps in the liver and skin.
sections.originalText: CASE DEFINITION:1, 2, 3, 4 | Vitiligo is a chronic, acquired autoimmune skin disorder characterized by well-demarcated hypopigmented or depigmented macules and patches resulting from the selective destruction of melanocytes in the epidermis. It may affect the skin, mucous membranes, and hair follicles, and can be associated with systemic autoimmune conditions such as thyroiditis, uveitis, and sensorineural hearing loss. | Before adressing vitiligo, it is important to understand the basic target cell that is affected by the disease and for that a basic overview of the melanin pathway is essential. Melanin is formed from the essential amino acids tyrosine and phenylalanine through a series of enzymatic steps in the liver and skin. Tyrosine is formed in the liver by the hydroxylation of the essential amino acid phenylalanine under the influence of phenylalanine hydroxylase which is in turn converted to DOPA and further into the pigment under the influence of tyrosinase enzyme (Fig. 1). The melanin is made within the melanosomes which are of two types —eumelanosomes (containing eumelanin), or pheomelanosomes (containing pheomelanin). These melanosomes pass into the dendritic processes of the melanocyte to be further transferred into neighboring keratinocytes.

sections.title: Ayurvedic Correlation
sections.content: Case Definition in Ayurveda: Shvitra is characterized by whitish, de-pigmented areas without exudation and non-infectious patches on the skin. The term Shvitra is a combination of Shweta and Rak. Shweta means whiteness, and Rak is a suffix of 'Shweta' Dhatu. The Nirukti of the term reveals white colour or changes toward white colour. Synonyms: Kilasa, Shweta, Shouklya, Aruna, and Daruna. In Ayurveda, nearly all skin conditions are classified generally as sub-varieties of Kustharoga and come under the general categories of “Kustharogadhikara” while a few are also described under “Kshudrarogadhikara”. However, among the different types of Kustha that are described in Brihattrayi, Shvitra has not been named as a subtype. But due to the Vaisishthaya (specificity) of the presentation, Shvitra is discussed separately in the Kustha chapter, which gives it particular attention.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Vitiligo, a common depigmenting skin disorder, has an estimated prevalence of 0.5–2% of the population worldwide. The prevalence of vitiligo is quite variable around the world, being more frequent in Africa (0.4%), Europe (0.4%), and Oceania (1.2%), than in North America (0.2%) and Asia (0.1%). In India, the reported prevalence of vitiligo ranges from approximately 0.5% to 2.5%, with some regional studies indicating even higher figures in specific populations. There is no difference in prevalence between races or genders. Females typically acquire the disease earlier than males. Onset may occur at any age, although about half of patients will have vitiligo by 20 years of age. It is broadly classified into nonsegmental vitiligo (NSV) and segmental (SV), with NSV being the most common form. Vitiligo significantly impacts patient's psychological and social well-being.

sections.title: Pathogenesis & Etiological Factors
sections.content: Updates in pathogenesis: Various theories have been propounded for the causation of vitiligo: 1. Genetic predisposition; 2. Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes; 3. Neural pathways (explains the stress and segmental type); 4. Metabolic abnormalities & oxidative stress - Accumulation of toxic metabolites and oxidants that damage melanocytes; 5. Self destruction of melanocytes (autocyto destructive). The autoimmune theory revolves around the role of CD8+ T-cells and T cells. The former is a cell that causes cell damage and the latter is a memory cell that leads to relapses. Formal studies have shown that biopsies of vitiligo show melanocyte destruction with presence of melanocyte specific CD8+ T-cells as compared to controls. These T-cells result in cell damage apoptosis via the release of IFN-γ which mediates its action via JAK/STAT pathway. Etiological Factors: Aaharaja (Dietary factors): Intake of incompatible food combinations (Virudha Ahara) such as milk with fish; Intake of unctuous and heavy-to-digest drinks (Snigdha-Guru Pana); Simultaneous intake of hot and cold potency foods and irregular fasting; Overeating, eating uncooked food, or eating before previous meal is digested; Excessive intake of freshly harvested grains, curd, fish, salt, and sour substances; Excessive intake of black gram (Masha), radish (Mulaka), sesame (Tila), and jaggery. Viharaja (Lifestyle factors): Suppression of natural urges like vomiting; Excessive physical exercise in hot weather or after a heavy meal; Use of cold water immediately after exposure to scorching sun, exertion, or during a frightening situation; Sleeping during daytime; Improper administration of Panchakarma therapies.

sections.title: Samprapti (Pathogenesis)
sections.content: The vitiated Doshas aggravated as a result of the indulgence in regular use of aggravating dietary and lifestyle factors and those particularly prone, as a result of specific Nidana, lead to the Sanga (obstruction) of the Rasavaha and Raktavaha srotasa. The aggravated Doshas vitiate the specific dhatu and result in the specific discoloration of the skin i.e. reddish, coppery or whitish, depending upon the Dhatu involved. The classics define Tritiya Twacha (the third layer of skin, as per Acharya Charaka) or Tamra (the fourth layer of the skin, as per Acharya Sushruta) to be the Adhisthana (site of occurrence) of the Kilasa. That is why the external as well as internal medication is required for Shvitra treatment.

sections.title: Clinical Presentation
sections.content: Vitiligo is clinically defined by the appearance of well-demarcated hypopigmented or depigmented macules and patches, resulting from the selective loss of functional melanocytes. These lesions are typically asymptomatic, though mild pruritus may occasionally be reported. In individuals with darker skin tones, the contrast between affected and unaffected areas is more pronounced. Lesion margins may exhibit intermediate hypopigmented zones, forming characteristic patterns such as trichrome or hypochromic vitiligo. Poliosis - depigmentation of hair within affected areas, often presenting as white locks on the scalp—is considered an indicator of deeper melanocyte involvement. Due to the absence of melanin, depigmented regions are more vulnerable to solar erythema. In cases of universal vitiligo, widespread depigmentation is observed. Additionally, lesions may develop at sites of skin trauma, a phenomenon known as koebnerization. An international consensus in 2011 standardized the classification of vitiligo, distinguishing segmental vitiligo (SV) from all other forms, which were grouped under non-segmental vitiligo (NSV). The consensus also introduced mixed vitiligo—coexistence of SV and NSV in a single patient—as a clinically distinct subgroup, categorized under NSV due to similar pathophysiological behaviour. Table no. 1: Expanded Classification — 1. Non-Segmental Vitiligo (NSV): Non-Segmental Vitiligo (NSV): The most prevalent form, presenting as bilaterally symmetrical depigmented patches. Commonly affected sites include periorificial regions (around the mouth, eyes), dorsal fingers, and intertriginous zones. Subtypes: Focal, Mucosal, Acrofacial, Generalized, Universal, Rare variants (e.g., leukoderma punctata, hypochromic vitiligo, follicular vitiligo). 2. Segmental Vitiligo (SV): Characterized by unilateral, localized depigmentation following a dermatomal pattern. It typically has an early onset, rapid stabilization, and limited progression, and is often resistant to conventional therapies. Subtypes: Focal, Unisegmental, Bi- or multisegmental. 3. Mixed Vitiligo: Involves the simultaneous presence of segmental and non-segmental lesions in the same individual. It may show asymmetric distribution and is important to recognize for therapeutic and prognostic considerations. Further classified by SV severity. 4. Unclassified Vitiligo: Includes atypical or early-stage cases that do not fit clearly into the above categories. Examples include focal lesions at onset, asymmetrical multifocal patches, or isolated mucosal involvement. Subtypes: Focal onset, Multifocal asymmetrical NSV, Isolated mucosal involvement. Clinical Presentation as per Ayurveda: The hallmark of Shvitra is presentation of the depigmented patches on the skin with the colour of the lesion differentiating the Dhatu dushti (vitiation of the tissues involved). E.g. Rakta varṇa (red colored lesions) in Rakta dhātudushti, Tāmravarṇa (copper-coloured lesions) in Māṁsadhātudushti, and Śvetavarṇa (whitish) due to Medo dhātudushti.

sections.title: Clinical Examination
sections.content: Important points of history that are helpful in the diagnosis of vitiligo include: Age at onset of lesions; Factors or events that may cause the onset of vitiligo; Symptoms associated with the lesions; Progression or spread of lesions; Changes observed in lesions over time; Presence of concomitant diseases; Current medications; Occupational history/ exposure to chemicals or radiation; Family history of vitiligo and autoimmune diseases. Physical Examination of vitiligo will include these features: The most affected areas include the face, neck, forearms, dorsal hands, fingers, feet, and scalp. On the face, lesions typically show a periocular or perioral distribution. In cases of generalized involvement, lesions may also be seen on the areolae, nipples, and genital region. Sites frequently exposed to friction or trauma—such as bony prominences (elbows, knees) are often involved, which may reflect the Koebner phenomenon, observed in 20–60% of vitiligo cases. Vitiligo manifests as depigmented macules or patches with a convex border without signs of inflammation with normal skin around. Macules are milky-white in color, well-demarcated with any shape. Ranges in size from a few millimeters to a few centimeters. Signs of other associated diseases may also be present like goiter, anemia, generalized wasting, premature grey hairs, alopecia areata and weakness, etc. Leukotrichia, or depigmentation of body hair within vitiliginous macules, may be noted during examination and is considered a marker of poor response to repigmentation therapies, as spontaneous recovery of pigment in affected hair is uncommon. Ayurvedic Clinical Examination: Not specified in this chapter.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis
sections.content: As has been depicted in the figures above the loss of melanocytes is not seen in many disorders and chemical leukoderma and piebaldism are the only two disorders that can be mistaken for vitiligo. Rests of the disorders are hypopigmented and not depigmented. Thus, the clinician should distinguish between these two entities. Table no. 2: The following diseases must be considered in differential diagnosis of Vitiligo — Chemically Induced Occupational Leukoderma; Drug-induced depigmentation; Genetic Syndromes (Hypomelanosis of Ito, Piebaldism, Waardenburg Syndrome, Tuberous sclerosis, Griscelli Syndrome, Hermansky–Pudlak Syndrome, Menkes Syndrome); Other Conditions (Lichen sclerosus et atrophicus, Tinea versicolor). Table no. 3: Differential Diagnosis in Ayurveda — Shvitra (वविरिठ): White patches; discoloration without much elevation; can be red, black, or white in early stages; may involve hair whitening (Romaśveta); dry, non-itchy or mildly itchy. Main pathology is Doṣhajadusṭi of Tvak, Rakta, Mamsa, Meda with Varṇa-vikāra (discoloration); absence of significant elevation, discharge, or pain. Kilasa (दकलास): White or black patches, more deeply rooted; three types (Aruṇa, Śveta, Śyāva); typically associated with stronger Kapha-Doṣa involvement and deeper involvement. Kustha (कुष्ठ): 18 types; includes Shvitra as one subtype; characterized by roughness, discoloration, itching, discharge, pain, and spreading. Shvitra is a Mahākustha, but other Kustha show more Śūla, Pāka, Srāva, and Dāha; also, more contagious and chronic. Paṇḍu (पाण्डु): Generalized pallor (not localized); includes Pāṇḍuta of skin, nails, eyes; associated with fatigue, edema, etc. Pāṇḍu is systemic and involves more than skin discoloration; Shvitra is localized to skin. Vyanga (व्यङ्ग): Bluish-black or dark brown pigmentation, mostly on face; due to emotions like anger or stress; no roughness or pain. Vyanga presents as dark patches rather than white; location and cause (Krodha, Śoka) are specific. Nilika (नीवलका): Bluish patches, due to vitiated Vata & Rakta; mostly painless, associated with burning. Unlike Shvitra which is white and painless, Nilika is painful and bluish. Arunshvitra/ Aruṇa-Kilasa: Pinkish red patches, more reddish and inflamed, with possible pain or oozing; intermediate between Shvitra and Kustha. Darunaka/ Sidhma: Scaly white eruptions on face or body; dry, slightly itchy; flakes easily. Presence of scaling (Rūkṣata, Kārśya) and less depigmentation; differentiates from smooth, white patches in Śvitra.

sections.title: Investigations
sections.content: While vitiligo is primarily diagnosed clinically, a skin biopsy may occasionally be performed to distinguish it from other hypopigmentary disorders. Further testing is indicated when signs or symptoms suggest other clinical conditions as associated autoimmune or endocrine conditions, such as thyroid disease, diabetes mellitus, pernicious anemia, Addison's disease, or alopecia areata. Table no. 4: Investigations may include — Detailed history and Physical examination; Complete Haemogram (A Complete haemogram can help detect abnormalities in blood cell counts that may indicate the associated conditions such as anaemia, or polycythemia, chronic infection or inflammations, etc.); Liver function test and Kidney Function test (Vitiligo is often associated with other autoimmune diseases, including thyroid disease, pernicious anemia, diabetes, and Addison's disease. Vitiligo is primarily diagnosed clinically, but Kidney Function Tests (KFT) and Liver Function Tests (LFT) are frequently included in the investigations to check for systemic autoimmune involvement, associated comorbidities, or to ensure safety before starting systemic treatments.). Advanced investigations — Wood's Lamp Examination (Especially helpful in fair-skinned individuals, this handheld UV light highlights vitiligo patches with a bright blue-white fluorescence, making early or subtle lesions easier to detect.); Thyroid panel: TSH, free T3, free T4 (Thyroid functional problems and autoimmune thyroid diseases have been linked to vitiligo. The two most significant and prevalent autoimmune thyroid conditions connected to vitiligo are Hashimoto thyroiditis and Graves' disease.); Antinuclear antibody (ANA) (ANAs are crucial for the identification of systemic autoimmune rheumatic disorders (SARDs) or any organ-specific autoimmune diseases.).

sections.title: Diagnostic Criteria
sections.content: Vitiligo is typically diagnosed clinically, based on the presence of acquired, amelanotic, non-scaly, chalky-white macules with well-defined margins. These lesions often follow characteristic distribution patterns, including periorificial areas, lips, distal extremities, genitalia, segmental zones, and sites of friction. Confirmatory laboratory investigations are generally unnecessary, except when required to rule out other differential diagnoses. Histopathological examination of the central portion of a vitiligo lesion reveals complete loss of melanin pigment in the epidermis and an absence of melanocytes. Occasionally, lymphocytic infiltration may be observed at the advancing margins of the lesions, suggesting active disease progression. Table no. 5: Assessment Tools for Extent and Severity — VASI (Vitiligo Area Scoring Index) (Widely used in clinical trials; validated for assessing extent and depigmentation.); VES (Vitiligo Extent Score) (Validated for clinical use and has high intra- and inter-rater reliability. Self-administered version (SA-VES) also validated.); VIDA (Vitiligo Disease Activity Score) (Simple clinical scale validated for assessing disease activity; Based on patient history.); VETF Score (Vitiligo European Task Force) (Comprehensive, validated scale used in research; include extent, stage, and spread.); DLQI (Dermatology Life Quality Index) (Broadly validated across dermatological conditions, including vitiligo.); Skindex-29 / Skindex-16 (Skin-specific QoL instruments; validated in vitiligo and other conditions.); VIS (Vitiligo Impact Scale) (Specifically developed and validated for assessing the psychosocial impact of vitiligo.). The clinical criteria for the diagnosis of segmental vitiligo: Essential criteria (major): Acquired depigmented macules occurring unilaterally not crossing the midline or with minimal spill onto the opposite side; Localized to a particular body area/site; Patterned distribution including recognizable patterns, viz., blaschkoid, dermatomal, phylloid, checkerboard, linear/oblong or any other specific type. Additional criteria (minor): Age at onset <15 years; Leucotrichia >50% over the affected lesion; Leucotrichia extending beyond the margin; Presence of islands of normal or hyperpigmentation within the lesion or segment without treatment; Margins >50% irregular/straight line; Stability achieved in disease progression by 1 year. Patients fulfilling all essential and one or more of the additional criteria are classified as segmental vitiligo and remaining patients as nonsegmental vitiligo. Diagnostic Criteria in Ayurveda: The involvement of the Doshas and Dhatus and their specific clinical presentations are the basic criteria for the diagnosis of Shvitra. Table no. 6: Prognosis — Criteria: Sadhya Lakshana vs Asadhya Lakshana — Nidana: Doshabalapravritti vs Adibalapravritti; Characteristics: Patches thin and pale, non confluent, Hair colour unchanged in vitiligo patches, No or Mild swelling vs Patches numerous and confluent/ merged, Hair colour changed in vitiligo patches to red or white or coppery; Chronicity: Duration < 1 year vs Duration > 1 year; Loci: Located on lips, palms, soles or genitalia; Cause: Caused by burn and wound.

sections.title: Principles of Management
sections.content: The principles of management include assessment of signs and symptoms before initiating treatment and the need for management through conventional treatment for associated comorbidities. If the patient is already under standard care, the physician may advise to continue the same along with add-on Ayurvedic treatment and can be assessed for the same in the follow ups for tapering or discontinue the treatment in consultation with the conventional physician. It must be noted that the therapy should address TWO key issues: 1. Repigmentation; 2. Stopping the Autoimmune process. As pigment cells are only present deep in the hair follicles, treatments mostly try to get melanocytes to divide and migrate into affected skin. The aims of vitiligo treatment are repigmentation and stabilization of the depigmentation process. In addition, agents that help to ameliorate the oxidative stress are a useful adjunct. The choice of therapy depends on the extent, location, and activity of disease as well as the patient's age, skin type and motivation to undergo treatment. In general, a period of at least 2–3 months is required to determine whether a particular treatment is effective. The areas of the body that typically have the best response to medical therapy are the face, neck, midextremities and trunk, while the distal extremities and lips are the most resistant to treatment.

The areas of the body that typically have the best response to medical therapy are the face, neck, midextremities and trunk, while the distal extremities and lips are the most resistant to treatment.

sections.title: Red Flag Signs
sections.content: These signs should be assessed before initiating treatment: Rapidly spreading or widespread depigmentation – suggests active disease needing early intervention; Poliosis (white hair in lesions) – Indicates deep melanocyte loss; often resistant to treatment; Mucosal or genital involvement – Associated with higher psychosocial impact and poor response; Onset after age 60 or in infants – Atypical; consider alternative diagnoses (e.g., lymphoma, post-inflammatory changes); Associated autoimmune diseases – Screen for thyroid, diabetes, etc.

sections.title: Preventive Treatment
sections.content: (A) Prevention: The prevention of vitiligo involves a three-tiered approach: Primary, Secondary, and Tertiary prevention. Primary prevention aims to reduce the risk of disease onset by avoiding known triggers such as skin trauma, chemical exposure, and excessive sunburn, while promoting immune health through stress management, a balanced antioxidant-rich diet, and healthy lifestyle practices. Secondary prevention focuses on early identification and prompt treatment to prevent disease progression, along with sun protection and regular monitoring using validated tools like the VIDA score. Tertiary prevention is directed toward managing established vitiligo, enhancing repigmentation through individualized therapy, addressing psychosocial concerns with counseling, improving cosmetic appearance, and monitoring for associated autoimmune conditions. Diet: Emerging evidence suggests that nutritional modulation may aid in vitiligo prevention and management by supporting melanocyte health and reducing oxidative stress. A diet rich in antioxidants, vitamins, and minerals is recommended. Recommended dietary components: Antioxidants (Vitamin C, E, β-carotene, selenium, zinc); Folic acid, Vitamin B12, and Copper (important for melanogenesis); Phytochemicals (from fruits, vegetables, green tea, turmeric). Lifestyle: Lifestyle practices that reduce physical and psychological stress are vital, as stress is a known trigger for vitiligo onset and progression. Avoidance of skin trauma (e.g., tight clothing, cosmetic irritants) to reduce Koebner phenomenon; Stress management techniques such as meditation, mindfulness, and counseling; Adequate sun protection to prevent photodamage of depigmented skin; Maintenance of sleep hygiene and regular circadian rhythms. Yoga: Yoga and related practices have shown beneficial effects in vitiligo, primarily through modulation of the immune system, stress reduction, and enhancement of systemic antioxidant status. Some of the practices found helpful are as follows: Pranayama (breathing exercises); Surya Namaskar (sun salutation); Shavasana, Yoga Nidra for relaxation; Meditation to reduce anxiety and autoimmune activation. (Proper guidance from a yoga expert is essential before practicing yoga for skin disorders).

sections.title: Shodhana (Curative)
sections.content: (B) Curative: Shodhana (Purification therapies): For Shodhana, generally Vamana (therapeutic emesis) and Virechana (therapeutic purgation) are used, and Basti (medicated enema) may be administered if necessary. After achieving proper purification (Samyak Shuddhi) and following the Samsarjana Krama (gradual dietary regimen), the following special therapeutic procedures are advised for the treatment of Shvitra (vitiligo). These procedures, when systematically administered, can lead to the desired formation of therapeutic eruptions or lesions (Sphotas). Special Shodhana in the Treatment of Shvitra (Vitiligo): Administration of Malpurasa* + mixed with Snuhi Ksheera** – For Sransana (3-4 days); Massage with mustard oil (Sarshapa Taila Abhyanga), followed by Surya Pada Santapa (exposure to sunlight); Only Peya (thin rice gruel) should be taken for 3 days (Taken whenever the patient feels thirsty); Formation of Eruptions (Sphota) on Shvitra Patches. When eruptions appear, they should be opened or punctured. Afterwards for 15 days: Daily morning intake of Kwatha (decoction) of Malpurasa, Vijayasara, Priyangu, and Shatapushpa or Palasha Kshara Kwatha with Phanit (sugarcane syrup). Kusthaghna herbs are beneficial and should be taken with or after Khadira Kwatha/Jala daily.

sections.title: Level 1 Treatment
sections.content: Line of treatment At level 1- (Solo Physician Clinic/Health & Health Clinic/PHC (Optimal Standard of treatment in situation where technology and resources are limited). Clinical Diagnosis: Clinical Criteria - Observation of well-demarcated, milky-white macules or patches. Check for symmetry, sensation and common sites (face, hands, genitals, etc.). Family History - Enquire about similar conditions in family. Provisional Diagnosis - Based on the history and presence of acquired depigmented patches. In most cases, no laboratory investigations are required unless there are clinical signs suggestive of associated autoimmune or endocrine disorders. Patient counselling, reassurance, and early initiation of treatment can be effectively initiated. Management: 1. Patient Assessment & Categorization - Evaluate disease severity, Doshic involvement, Agni, and systemic signs. Table no. 9: Examination of Dosha Involvement: Clinical Features — Dryness, roughness, blackish edge → Vāta; Redness, burning, inflammation → Pitta; White thick patches, itching, heaviness → Kapha; Mixed features → Sannipāta. Table no. 10: Examination of Agni: Agni Type — Samāgni (Normal digestion, clear belching, no heaviness); Viṣamāgni (Irregular digestion, sometimes strong/sometimes weak appetite); Tīkṣṇāgni (Fast digestion, excessive hunger, burning sensation); Mandāgni (Slow digestion, heaviness, bloating, dull appetite). Table no. 11: Examination of Ama: Signs & Symptoms — Coated tongue; Heaviness post-meals; Loss of appetite; Sticky, foul-smelling stools; General fatigue, malaise. Categorize patient as: Requires Shodhana → Refer to Level 2 or Level 3 Ayurvedic hospital. Provide case summary and referral note. Suitable for Shamana only → Counsel the patient: Shvitra is manageable and non-contagious; Emphasize diet/lifestyle adherence and regular treatment; Prescribe treatment as per Table 7. Select oral and local therapies based on Dosha, lesion site, and strength. Follow up: Review every 15–30 days. Referral Criteria: Uncertain Diagnosis – Atypical presentation or diagnostic confusion with other hypopigmented disorders (e.g., leprosy, pityriasis alba, tinea versicolor); Rapid Progression – Sudden and extensive spread of depigmented lesions; Mucosal or Extensive Involvement – Vitiligo affecting genital mucosa, lips, eyelids, or involving 10% of body surface area; Severe Psychological Distress – Evidence of anxiety, depression, or social withdrawal due to cosmetic impact; Unresponsive to Initial Management – No improvement after a reasonable period of individualized care; Suspected Associated Autoimmune Disorders – Presence of signs suggestive of thyroid disease, diabetes, or adrenal insufficiency requiring investigation and specialist input; Uncontrolled comorbidities; Evidence of an increase in severity/complications; Substantial impact on their quality of life and activities of daily living.

sections.title: Level 2 & Level 3 Treatment
sections.content: At Level 2- (CHC/Small hospitals (10-20 bedded hospitals with basic facilities such as routine, investigation, X-ray). Clinical Diagnosis: The case referred from Level 1, or a fresh case must be evaluated thoroughly. Investigations: The diagnosis would be primarily clinical along with some investigations which will be necessary to investigate complications or exclude other differential diagnoses as follows: Complete Haemogram. Management: Clinical Evaluation: Assess extent and stage of lesions, Dosha involvement, Agni, Aama, and systemic symptoms. Review previous treatments and response. Categorization: Shodhana required: Moderate to severe cases, chronic or Bahu Dosha Avastha; Shamana suitable: Mild, localized, early-stage cases. Shodhana Administration: Panchakarma procedures like Virechana (therapeutic purgation). Shamana Chikitsa Protocol: Patient Counselling on non-contagious nature and treatability of Shvitra. Initiate Treatment: Use medicines as per standard protocol (Table 7). Combine internal medications with local therapies (Lepa, Suryapadsantap, etc.). Simple Raktamokshana may be done if expertise is available. Follow-Up: Review every 15–30 days. Referral Criteria: Patients at Level 2 should be referred to higher centers under the following conditions: Same as mentioned earlier at level 1, plus No clinical improvement or worsening despite appropriate homoeopathic management; Complications requiring advanced diagnostic tools or specialty care; Need for multidisciplinary evaluation or emergency care; Non-responsiveness in suspected autoimmune, systemic, or rapidly progressing pathology; Diagnostic uncertainty requires investigation beyond the available infrastructure; Referral should be made to Ayush Level 3 or appropriate higher-level healthcare facilities with specialist services and comprehensive diagnostic setups; Any other complications that threaten the life of the patient. Level 3- (Ayush hospitals attached with teaching Institution, District Level/ Integrated/ State Ayush Hospitals). Clinical Diagnosis: Same as Level 1 & 2. Confirm diagnosis and severity with the help of investigations such as: Thyroid function tests (TSH, fT3, fT4), anti-thyroid antibodies, ANA, fasting glucose levels, HbA1c. Wood's lamp examination can be used to enhance the visibility of depigmented lesions, particularly in fair-skinned individuals or early-stage disease. If needed, differential diagnosis from other hypopigmented conditions (e.g., pityriasis versicolor, post-inflammatory hypopigmentation) can be aided by routine investigations and clinical pattern recognition. (In case of clinical suspicion or doubt). Management Protocol: Panchakarma Therapy: Based on Dosha predominance, disease chronicity, and patient's Bala: Vamana; Virechana; Basti; Raktamokshana (Consider the table below to prescribe the appropriate method). Table No.12: Types of Raktamokshana and its details — S. No. Type of Method Used: Indications / Dominant Doṣa / Preferred Sites Involved / Remarks — 1 Sirāvedha (Venesection): Chronic, large lesions; deep-seated Doṣa vitiation; Pitta-Rakta; Forearm, dorsal foot, cephalic vein; Quick and potent; avoid in debilitated patients. 2 Jalauka- Leech Avacharaṇa: Pitta-Kapha; Face, neck; Pitta type Śvitra with burning or reddish patches; Gentle; suitable for children, elderly, soft or delicate skin. 3 Prachchhanna with blade: Localized Kapha-Rakta; Directly over affected lesion; Kapha patches with stable lesions; Mild; good for superficial symptoms. 4 Alabu (Cupping with dried gourd): Slightly raised, thickened lesions with Kapha dominance; Kapha; Shoulders, limbs; Improves local circulation and lymphatic drainage. 5 Śṛṅga (Horn-based cupping): Deeper lesions, Vāta-Kapha; Vāta-Kapha; Back, thighs; Traditional method; requires skilled application. 6 Ghaṭī Yantra (Metallic cupping): When Kapha is weak or thin; stronger Vāta suction is needed than Alabu; Arms, back, flanks; Powerful; not suitable for very weak patients. Internal Medication: Use medicines as per standard protocol (Table 7). Combine internal medications with local therapies (lepa, suryapadsantap, etc.). Rasayana Therapy: Post-shodhana or with long-term shamana therapy to restore melanocyte function. Use of drugs like Chyawanprash, Amalaki Rasayana, or specific tailor-made Rasayana compounds. Local Applications & Procedures: Bakuchi taila or Lepa yogas with phototherapy (controlled sun exposure or UV lamps if available). Diet & Lifestyle Advice: Continue Ahara-Vihara counselling tailored to dosha and patient constitution. Follow-Up: First Month: Follow up every 7–10 days; Check treatment response and adjust if needed. 1 to 3 Months: Follow up every 15 days; Monitor pigmentation and lesion changes. 3 to 6 Months: Follow up once a month; Continue medicines, Rasayana, and lifestyle advice. After 6 Months: Follow up every 2–3 months; Watch for relapse and give long-term guidance. Referral Criteria: Same as mentioned earlier at level 2 plus Other therapeutic modalities—such as counseling, yoga, dietary modifications, or integrative Ayush approaches etc.—may be considered based on the complexity and individualized needs of the patient. In select cases, referral to higher centers may also be appropriate for psychological reassurance or cosmetic interventions.

sections.title: Clinical Algorithm
sections.content: ALGORITHM FOR TREATMENT FOR SHVITRA: SHVITRA → If Shamana only is Required → Assess Sadhya-Asadhyata → Nidan Parivarjana: Every patient shall be assessed for probable nidana (etiological factors) and instructed to avoid them and to follow pathya → Sadhya Shvitra / Asadhya Shvitra → Pratyakheya Purvak Chikitsa → Level 1 → Small/localized patient and few patches → Examine the patient → Shaman Chikitsa or both as applicable → Multiple/generalised patches → If Shodhana Is Also Required → Shaman Chikitsa → Level 2 or 3 → Shodhana* + Shaman Chikitsa → Special Shodhana Chikitsa mentioned for Shvitra: Followed by Shaman Chikitsa → Continue for 21 days → Improvement Yes → Continue the Treatment; Improvement No → (continue/reassess). *Perform shodhana only after considering rogi bala and roga bala.

sections.content: Vitiligo is manageable and non-contagious. Emphasize diet/lifestyle adherence and regular treatment. Counsel the patient about the non-contagious nature and treatability of Shvitra. Sun protection is important to prevent photodamage of depigmented skin.
